t: Minimum Swaps to Make Strings Equal — Counting Mismatch Pairs
o: We may only swap characters between the two strings, and we want both strings identical at every index. Only indices where `s1[i] != s2[i]` matter — at those positions the pair is either `(x,y)` or `(y,x)`; call their counts `a` and `b`. A single swap can fix **two** mismatches of the same type: swapping `s1[i]` with `s2[j]` when both are `(x,y)` turns them into `(y,x)`... more precisely it makes both positions match. So same-type mismatches pair up for free. If one `(x,y)` and one `(y,x)` remain, they cost exactly 2 swaps (as in Example 2). If the total number of mismatched positions is odd, some position has an unfixable parity — return -1 (Example 3 has one mismatch, total = 1, odd → -1). With n ≤ 1000 even an O(n²) scan is fine, but O(n) counting is trivial.
k: Only mismatched positions matter; each is either type 'xy' (s1=x, s2=y) or type 'yx'.
Two mismatches of the same type are fixed by 1 swap; one of each type costs 2 swaps.
If the number of mismatched positions is odd, the answer is -1.

a.i: Scan left to right keeping a buffer of unresolved mismatches of each type. Whenever we see a mismatch whose opposite type is pending, resolve both with one swap conceptually; otherwise record it. At the end, leftover singles of each type combine into one cross-type pair costing 2 swaps. This mirrors how you'd fix things by hand and leads directly to the closed-form formula.
s: Iterate over all indices; skip positions where s1[i] == s2[i].
Count a = number of (x,y) mismatches, b = number of (y,x) mismatches.
a.t: O(n) — one pass over the strings plus constant-time arithmetic.

a.n: Approach 2: BFS on Mismatch States (conceptual baseline)
a.i: Treat each mismatched index's state ('xy' or 'yx') as part of a search problem: from any state, applying a swap changes at most two states, and we BFS for the minimum number of swaps to reach zero mismatches. The state space collapses because only counts (a, b) matter, giving transitions (a,b) → (a-2,b), (a,b-2), (a-1,b+1), (a+1,b-1). BFS over these few reachable states confirms the formula: distance = a/2 + b/2 + (a%2)*2 when a+b is even. It's mainly useful to justify why the greedy formula is optimal — each swap reduces the mismatch count by at most 2, so pairing same types first is optimal.
s: Reduce the problem to the pair of counters (a, b).
BFS from (a, b); neighbors come from swapping across any two mismatched positions.
Return the BFS depth when reaching (0, 0); unreachable means -1.
The resulting distances match the closed-form a/2 + b/2 + (a%2)*2.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to count, then BFS explores only O(a·b) tiny counter-states (in practice constant-bounded by n/2 each, so worst case O(n²) states, but the formula shortcut makes it effectively O(n)).
a.sp: O(n²) worst case for the visited set of counter-states; O(1) extra if you just use the derived formula.

w: In an interview, present the counting formula directly: answer = a/2 + b/2 + (a%2)*2, or -1 when a+b is odd — it's optimal and trivially implementable in one pass. Use the BFS framing only to argue optimality (each swap fixes at most 2 mismatches, so pairing same-type mismatches first is best). Common pitfalls: forgetting that a lone 'xy' plus a lone 'yx' costs 2 swaps, not 1; miscomputing the impossibility condition (it's about the *total* mismatch count being odd, not a or b individually); and off-by-one issues when a or b is odd. Edge cases: strings already equal (answer 0), single-character strings, all mismatches of one type. Follow-ups might ask to generalize to alphabets larger than {x, y} (then you need cycle-decomposition arguments) or to output the actual swap sequence.
